name: Fairy Flag

attributes.attribute: came to this world to be with him

sources: MacGregor, Alasdair Alpin. The Peat-Fire Flame: Folk-Tales and Traditions of the Highlands & Islands. Edinburgh: The Moray Press, 1937, 20+.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text:
The Fairy Flag is a celebrated object in Scottish folklore. It is preserved at Dunvegan Castle, the seat of the MacLeod clan on the Isle of Skye. Accounts call it one of the most treasured sights of the fairy realm.

One legend tells of an autumn night. A woman dressed in green went into the castle nursery. She found the heir asleep and the nurse dozing. Strangers were normally suspected of intending an abduction of the child. Instead the woman simply sat and hummed a tune known as "Taladh na Mna Sithe", the lullaby of the fairy woman. The nurse came awake but feared to act. She watched the visitor wrap the boy in silk, then vanish. The child stayed safe.

The nurse carried the boy to his parents. Their attention went to the odd blanket, which became the banner of the MacLeods. It was thought to guard the clan in war, and every nursery nurse was required to know the lullaby that guarded the children.

Other tales give the flag other origins. In one, a woman of the Holy Land gave it to the MacLeods. She said that when the cloth was unrolled it cast a spell that made every fighting man look like a full unit. In another, a fairy woman came to court a clan chief. She found she could not live apart from her own land, so she left. She gave him the flag as a parting token.

okr.objective: The Fairy Flag is a famed Scottish relic that shields the MacLeod clan.
key_results: The Fairy Flag is kept at Dunvegan Castle, which belongs to the MacLeods on the Isle of Skye.
A green-clad fairy woman once wrapped the infant heir in a silken garment in the nursery.
The flag is said to make each MacLeod soldier seem like a whole battalion.
A fairy woman left the banner behind when she could not stay with a MacLeod chief.
